subject: 약속과 계약의 도덕적 차이
title: Promises and contracts as moral acts
content: A promise and a contract both bind, and yet moral philosophy treats them as different in kind rather than in degree. A contract is enforceable, so a party who breaks one faces a remedy the law supplies, whereas a promise carries no such backing and binds only through the moral claim it creates. This difference is easy to state and harder to explain, because it is unclear why adding enforcement should change the character of an obligation at all. One view holds that the difference lies in what each act does. A promise transfers a right directly to the person promised, so the wrong of breaking it is a wrong to her, whereas a contract creates a relationship the law will police, and the wrong is partly against the order that guarantees it. Both accounts allow for moral failure, although they locate it differently. A second view is more sceptical, treating contracts as promises that happen to be written down. Its defenders argue that enforcement changes what a party can get away with rather than what she owes, and that the moral situation was fixed when the agreement was made. Critics reply that this ignores how the availability of enforcement alters what people reasonably expect of one another, since a promise made where no remedy exists asks for a trust that a contract does not.

subject: 무지의 도덕적 책임
title: Moral responsibility for what one does not know
content: We ordinarily excuse people for harms they could not have foreseen, and yet ignorance sometimes makes a person more blameworthy rather than less. A driver who did not know his brakes were failing is excused where the fault was hidden, and he is not excused where he had been warned and chose not to look. Moral philosophy therefore asks when ignorance excuses and when it aggravates. The traditional answer looks backward to an earlier moment of control. If a person could have known and had reason to find out, then her later ignorance traces to a failure she is answerable for, and the excuse dissolves. This account fits the driving case well, since the duty to check brakes is clear enough. Its difficulty is that many culpable failures of knowledge cannot be traced to any particular moment when the agent decided not to inquire. A second approach abandons the search for that moment and asks instead what the person's ignorance reveals about what she cared for. Someone who never notices the harm she causes to a group displays an indifference that is itself a moral fault, whatever the history of her inattention. Critics object that this blames people for their upbringing, and defenders answer that moral character is exactly what blame has always tracked.

subject: 중세 흑해 연안의 정착과 문화 접촉
title: Settlement and contact on the medieval Black Sea coast
content: Excavation along the medieval Black Sea coast reveals settlements whose material culture cannot be assigned to any single tradition. Pottery from several regions appears in the same layers, buildings combine techniques from the steppe and from the Mediterranean, and the cemeteries hold burials following different rites within a few paces of one another. These sites therefore record contact rather than any one people. What the layers show over time is neither replacement nor blending but a persistent mixture. A quarter that used one style of vessel in the ninth century still uses it in the eleventh while a neighbouring quarter uses another, and neither disappears. This pattern suggests that communities kept their own practices while living side by side, and that the coast functioned as a place where groups met without merging. Written sources from the period say little about these settlements, since the chroniclers who wrote about the region were interested in rulers rather than in coastal towns. Archaeologists therefore work almost entirely from what was dug, and the picture they reconstruct differs considerably from the political narrative. Where the chronicles describe a frontier between powers, the excavated evidence describes a zone of ordinary and continuous exchange.

subject: 설계와 우연 — 목적론적 설명의 지위
title: Purpose and chance in explanation
content: Saying that the heart exists in order to pump blood attributes a purpose, and philosophy has long asked whether such statements describe anything real or merely reflect how we find it convenient to speak. The question matters because purposive language is indispensable in biology while seeming out of place in physics, and any account of explanation must say why. One tradition treats purpose talk as shorthand for a causal history. The heart has the effect it does because ancestors with hearts that pumped left more descendants, so the apparent purpose is a compressed description of selection. On this view nothing beyond ordinary causation is asserted, although the shorthand remains useful because it captures a pattern that would take many sentences to state. A rival tradition holds that the shorthand does genuine explanatory work. Knowing what a trait is for tells us which of its many effects account for its presence, and that distinction cannot be recovered from a list of causes alone. Both sides agree that purposes require no designer, and their disagreement concerns whether functional explanation adds something to causal explanation or merely abbreviates it. The dispute has practical weight in medicine, where calling a condition a malfunction presupposes an answer.

subject: 전쟁에서의 비례성 원칙
title: Proportionality in the ethics of war
content: The moral tradition governing warfare holds that harm inflicted must be proportionate to the good achieved, and this requirement sounds clear until one attempts to apply it. Proportion is a relation between two quantities, and here the quantities are of different kinds, since one side of the comparison holds deaths and the other holds a political objective. No common measure exists, so the judgment cannot be a calculation. Defenders of the principle accept this and argue that it still does moral work. Even without a scale, some comparisons are obvious, and a campaign that destroys a city to secure a minor advantage is plainly disproportionate whatever the difficulty of precise measurement. The principle rules out the clear cases and constrains argument in the unclear ones, which is more than nothing. Critics answer that a standard which decides only the obvious cases leaves the contested ones to whoever is making the decision, and that in practice the party inflicting the harm is also the party judging the proportion. They add that the objective is typically described by that same party, so both terms of the comparison are supplied by an interested judge. Whether an independent standard is possible remains the central question in this part of moral philosophy.

subject: 베네치아 석호 정착과 도시의 형성
title: Settling a lagoon and building a medieval city
content: The settlement of the Venetian lagoon began as refuge rather than as design, and the archaeological evidence shows communities occupying scattered islands of firm ground amid marsh. Building on such a site required driving timber piles into the mud until they met a stable layer, and the excavated foundations preserve those piles in remarkable condition, since waterlogged ground keeps wood that dry ground would destroy. What the earliest layers record is dispersal. Separate island communities each had their own church and their own landing, and only later do the excavations show the channels dredged and the bridges built that joined them into a single medieval settlement. The physical unification of the city was therefore an achievement of centuries rather than a founding act, and the shape of the modern streets still follows the older separate parishes. Maintaining the site demanded continuous work. Channels silted, piles decayed above the waterline, and the surrounding marsh had to be managed so that neither erosion nor deposition closed the lagoon. Medieval records describe offices charged with exactly these tasks, and archaeologists find their interventions in the sediment. Historians accordingly treat this city as a case where the environment was neither obstacle nor gift but a permanent undertaking.

subject: 유전적 개입의 윤리적 경계
title: Moral limits on genetic intervention
content: Correcting a genetic condition that would otherwise cause suffering seems morally continuous with medicine, and enhancing a trait that is already within the normal range seems different in a way that many people find difficult to articulate. Moral philosophy has therefore examined whether the distinction between treatment and enhancement can bear the weight placed upon it. The distinction requires a baseline of normal functioning, and defining that baseline turns out to involve judgments about what a good human life includes. Where the line falls has shifted historically as medicine has changed what it can do, which suggests that the boundary reflects our expectations rather than any natural division. Critics of the distinction conclude that it cannot ground a moral difference. Defenders reply that a criterion may be vague and still be useful, since many moral distinctions admit borderline cases without collapsing. A separate concern applies to interventions that would be inherited, because those affect people who cannot consent and who will live under conditions chosen for them. That objection does not depend on the treatment distinction at all, and it applies with equal force to corrections and to enhancements. Much recent work argues that this second concern is the more serious one, and that the debate over enhancement has drawn attention away from it.

subject: 중세 지중해의 난파와 항해 관습
title: Wrecks and sailing custom in the medieval Mediterranean
content: Medieval wrecks excavated in the Mediterranean preserve details of sailing practice that no written source records. The arrangement of their ballast, the placement of their cooking hearths, and the personal possessions found in their sterns all indicate how a vessel was lived in as well as how it was loaded. Because a wreck freezes a single voyage, archaeologists can reconstruct what a crew carried for itself rather than what it carried for sale. Hull construction changed during these centuries, and the excavated remains date that change precisely. Earlier vessels were built shell first, with their planks joined edge to edge and their frames inserted afterward, whereas later ones were built frame first with planks fastened to a skeleton. This second method required less skilled labour and less timber, and the transition appears in wrecks across the medieval period rather than at any single moment. Where a vessel went down also reflects custom. Ships hugged their coasts and anchored at night in the earlier centuries, so these wrecks cluster near headlands and harbours, whereas later vessels crossed open water and their remains lie in deeper places that only recent survey has reached. Historians reading this distribution treat it as evidence about confidence and navigation rather than merely about where the sea is dangerous.

subject: 동물 실험의 정당화 조건
title: When experiments on animals can be justified
content: Research on animals causes suffering to creatures that cannot consent, and it is defended by the benefits it brings to humans and sometimes to animals themselves. Moral philosophy has examined whether this defence succeeds, and the examination turns on what moral weight the interests of the subjects carry. If those interests count for nothing, no justification is needed; if they count as much as ours, almost no experiment could be justified at all. Almost nobody holds either extreme, so the real question is what a graded position permits. Positions that assign animals substantial but lesser weight must explain the discount, and appeals to species membership are widely regarded as arbitrary since they name a biological fact rather than a morally relevant one. Appeals to cognitive capacity avoid that objection while implying that humans of comparable capacity could be used in the same way, which almost everyone rejects. A regulatory consensus has developed that requires minimizing numbers, reducing suffering, and replacing animal subjects where alternatives exist. These requirements are defensible on any graded view, and their acceptance does not settle the underlying question. Philosophers note that a framework everyone can accept may function to postpone the disagreement rather than to resolve it.

subject: 역사적 부정의에 대한 보상
title: Repairing historical injustice
content: Claims for redress arising from wrongs committed generations ago raise moral questions that ordinary compensation does not, because the parties who acted and the parties who suffered are no longer present. If compensation restores a victim to the position she would have occupied, then the death of that victim seems to end the claim, and yet many people judge that something is still owed. Moral philosophy has tried to explain why. One approach traces the injustice forward through its effects. A wrong that stripped a community of land or education produces disadvantages that persist across generations, so the present claim concerns present harm with a historical cause rather than a debt inherited from the dead. This avoids the difficulty about parties while raising a hard question about which present inequalities can be traced. A second approach locates the wrong in a continuing failure of acknowledgement. On this view what is owed is recognition rather than restoration, and an apology that names the wrong accomplishes something that a payment does not. Critics reply that acknowledgement without material change is cheap, and defenders answer that material change without acknowledgement misdescribes what happened. Most substantial proposals combine the two, which suggests that neither captures the whole of what such claims assert.

subject: 고대 페르시아의 관개 지하수로
title: Underground water channels of ancient Persia
content: Ancient communities on the Iranian plateau reached groundwater by cutting tunnels that ran for many kilometres from a mother well at the foot of the hills to their outlet in the fields below. Their gradient had to fall gently enough that the flow would not scour the channel, and steeply enough that it would not silt, so surveying that gradient underground without instruments was the central difficulty. Vertical shafts sunk at intervals let spoil be lifted and air reach the workers, and these shafts are what a modern survey sees from the air as lines of craters. Their construction was slow and dangerous, so a completed channel represented an investment of years by a community or its patron. Because this water flowed by gravity and required no lifting, the system delivered a constant supply at almost no running cost, and channels cut in antiquity were still flowing in recent centuries. Maintenance rather than construction determined their survival. A tunnel that lost its cleaning crews collapsed within a few seasons, and the archaeological record shows districts where whole systems failed together during periods of disruption. Historians therefore read the presence of working channels as evidence of continuous social organization rather than merely of ancient engineering.

subject: 자기 이익과 도덕적 이유
title: Self-interest and moral reasons
content: A person who asks why she should be moral when morality conflicts with her interest is raising a question that has troubled philosophy since antiquity. The question is not easily dismissed, since telling her that the action is required simply restates what she is querying, and telling her that she will be caught changes the subject to prudence. What she wants is a reason that engages her as she is. One classical answer denies the conflict. On this view a person who acts unjustly damages herself, because a life organized around getting the better of others is disordered and cannot go well, so morality and interest converge when interest is properly understood. The argument is attractive and difficult to establish, since it must show that every immoral act harms its author, and the cases where wrongdoing plainly pays are the ones that most need explaining. A second answer accepts the conflict and denies that it undermines morality. Moral reasons are reasons whether or not they serve the agent, and a demand that they be reducible to self-interest assumes what the sceptic set out to prove. Its cost is that no argument remains for someone who acknowledges the reason and declines to be moved, and philosophers disagree about whether such a person is unreasonable or merely bad.
